Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Working diagnosis and impressions: Probable knee overuse injury with potential meniscal involvement and/or patellofemoral pain syndrome; early degenerative changes possible given age and activity; no current knee effusion or instability on exam described in transcript, but persistent activity-related symptoms warrant formal assessment.
- Relevant differential diagnoses and reasoning (consistent with transcript and DDx):
  - Meniscal tear (traumatic or degenerative) — supports clicking, activity-related pain, prior knee trauma; high likelihood given transcript data.
  - Patellofemoral pain syndrome / chondromalacia patellae — supports pain with bending/loading, running, and crepitus; high likelihood.
  - Osteoarthritis of the knee (degenerative) — possible in a 45-year-old with overuse; medium likelihood.
  - Iliotibial band syndrome — possible in runners; medium likelihood.
  - Traumatic ligament injuries (ACL/MCL) — considered given prior ice hockey fall; low likelihood due to current absence of instability or locking on exam.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: Not observed; no conflict noted.
- Management priorities: Confirm pathology with clinical assessment, consider imaging if indicated, initiate conservative management, and arrange specialist input.

Management Plan

- Ice therapy: Continue ice application to the knee to reduce inflammation after activity.
- Activity modification: Ease up on running; avoid painful activities; resume gradually as tolerated.
- Medications: Continue ibuprofen as needed; consider a prescription NSAID with better systemic control, to be used regularly and not in combination with ibuprofen; ensure dosing is with food.
- Imaging/consultation: Refer to physiotherapist for a comprehensive knee assessment and rehabilitation plan; imaging (e.g., MRI) considered if persistent pain, swelling, heat, redness, fever, or mechanical symptoms (locking) develop; clinic evaluation if wait times are long.
- Follow-up and red flags: If persistent swelling, heat, redness, fever, or knee locking with inability to bend/straighten, seek urgent medical evaluation promptly.
- Patient education: Ice therapy benefits healing; modify training plan to prevent overuse injuries; consider gradual return-to-run strategies; discuss that definitive diagnosis requires physical examination and possibly imaging.

- Allied health referral (EPC – 10 visits):  Yes – referral to physiotherapist discussed/arranged
- Reproductive or sexual health clinic referral: Not recorded
- Mental health support if indicated (e.g., psychologist, AMS support): Not recorded
- CTG registration: Not recorded
- Preventive health follow-up booked (e.g., flu vaccine, Pap test): Not recorded

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

- Meniscal tear (traumatic or degenerative)
  - Likelihood: High
  - Justification: Joint-line clicking with knee flexion/extension; activity-related pain beginning after several minutes of running; prior knee injury; transient swelling after initial episode; full ROM currently preserved.
- Patellofemoral pain syndrome / chondromalacia patellae
  - Likelihood: High
  - Justification: Pain with knee bending and loading during running; mid-knee pain with movement; crepitus noted; runner overuse pattern.
- Osteoarthritis of the knee (degenerative)
  - Likelihood: Medium
  - Justification: Age ~45 with overuse activity and mechanical knee pain; intermittent symptoms; absence of morning stiffness or systemic inflammatory signs.
- Iliotibial band syndrome (ITBS)
  - Likelihood: Medium
  - Justification: Running-related knee pain; onset with increased running; however, lateral knee pain location not specified in transcript.
- ACL/MCL injury or other ligamentous injury (traumatic)
  - Likelihood: Low
  - Justification: Mechanism includes a fall on ice; current exam shows no instability or locking; still considered given trauma history.
